rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which one of the following first row transition elements is expected to have the highest third ionization enthalpy ?
rows.solution:
MANGANESE has the highest third ionisation enthalpy.

The third ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove an electron from the \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion, so the question is really about which \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion is the most reluctant to lose one.

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^5\) — an exactly HALF-FILLED subshell, which carries extra stability from the exchange energy of five parallel electrons. Removing a sixth electron would break that arrangement up, so it costs unusually much.

The other three have no such advantage: \(\mathrm{V^{2+}}\) is \(3d^3\), \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is \(3d^4\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Iron is the useful contrast — losing an electron from \(3d^6\) PRODUCES the stable \(3d^5\), so its third ionisation enthalpy is unusually LOW, which is why iron(III) is so common.

rows.stem: Which of the following compounds will give a ketone on oxidation with chromic anhydride \(\mathrm{(CrO_3)}\) ?
rows.solution:
The compound giving a ketone is \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(OH)CH_3}\), butan-2-ol.

What an oxidising agent produces depends entirely on the CLASS of alcohol. A SECONDARY alcohol has one hydrogen on the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group; removing that hydrogen and the hydroxyl hydrogen gives a carbon-oxygen double bond with two carbon substituents — a KETONE.

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(OH)CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2COCH_3}\)

The other three cannot. Both \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHCH_2OH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\) are PRIMARY and give an aldehyde, which is oxidised on to a carboxylic acid. And \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C{-}OH}\) is TERTIARY — it has NO hydrogen on the carbinol carbon at all, so it resists oxidation entirely unless the conditions are drastic enough to break a carbon-carbon bond.

rows.stem: Two among the three components of DNA are \(\beta\)-D-2-deoxyribose and a heterocyclic base. The third component is :
rows.solution:
The third component is PHOSPHORIC ACID.

A nucleic acid is built from repeating NUCLEOTIDES, and each nucleotide has three parts: a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base, and a PHOSPHATE group derived from phosphoric acid. The base joins the sugar at \(\mathrm{C_1}\), and the phosphate joins it at \(\mathrm{C_5}\), the phosphate then linking one sugar to the next to build the backbone of the strand.

Of the distractors, adenine and uracil are BASES, not a third kind of component — and uracil would be wrong for DNA in any case, since DNA carries thymine where RNA carries uracil. Sulphuric acid has no place in a nucleic acid at all.

rows.stem: For an electrolyte undergoing association in a solvent, the van't Hoff factor :
rows.solution:
For an electrolyte undergoing ASSOCIATION, the van't Hoff factor is ALWAYS LESS THAN ONE.

The factor is defined as the ratio of the number of particles ACTUALLY present in solution to the number expected from the formula:
\(i = \dfrac{\text{observed number of particles}}{\text{expected number of particles}}\)

Association means molecules are combining with one another — two molecules of acetic acid joining into one dimer in benzene, for instance — so the observed count falls BELOW the expected one, and the ratio comes out under 1.

Dissociation does the opposite and gives \(i > 1\). The factor is a ratio of two counts, so it can never be zero or negative.

The consequence is measurable: an associating solute produces a SMALLER depression in freezing point than its formula predicts.

rows.stem: For the reaction \(\mathrm{X} + 2\mathrm{Y} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}\), the differential form equation of the rate law is :
rows.solution:
For \(\mathrm{X} + 2\mathrm{Y} \longrightarrow \mathrm{P}\), the correct relation is \(\dfrac{2\,\mathrm{d[P]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = \dfrac{-\,\mathrm{d[Y]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\).

Build the rate expression from the stoichiometry. Each species is divided by its coefficient, reactants taking a minus sign because they are being consumed:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d[X]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[Y]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = +\dfrac{\mathrm{d[P]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

Taking the last two terms and clearing the fraction:
\(-\dfrac{\mathrm{d[Y]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = 2\dfrac{\mathrm{d[P]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

which is the option chosen. The physical content is that \(\mathrm{Y}\) disappears TWICE as fast as \(\mathrm{P}\) appears, because two molecules of it are consumed for each molecule of product.

The option that puts the 2 on the \(\mathrm{Y}\) side instead has the ratio inverted, and the two options with matching signs on a reactant and a product are wrong on sign alone.

rows.stem: The compound which undergoes \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction most rapidly is :

options.label: A
options.text: A six-membered carbon ring carrying ONE \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond, with \(\mathrm{Br}\) bonded to a ring carbon (drawn skeletal structure)

options.label: B
options.text: A fully saturated six-membered carbon ring bonded to \(\mathrm{-CH_2-Br}\) (drawn skeletal structure)

options.label: C
options.text: A fully saturated six-membered carbon ring with \(\mathrm{Br}\) bonded to a ring carbon (drawn skeletal structure)

options.label: D
options.text: A six-membered carbon ring carrying THREE alternating \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bonds, with \(\mathrm{Br}\) bonded to a ring carbon (drawn skeletal structure)

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — ALL FOUR OPTIONS ARE DRAWN SKELETAL STRUCTURES; the stem names nothing, so the drawings ARE the question. Read at 8x: (A) a hexagon with Br at its right vertex and a single inner double-bond line along the BOTTOM edge, i.e. the double bond lies between the two carbons two bonds round from the Br-bearing carbon; (B) a plain hexagon joined to CH2-Br; (C) a plain hexagon joined directly to Br; (D) a Kekule benzene hexagon (three inner double-bond lines) joined to Br. The option texts above describe the drawings without naming the compounds, so the discrimination the question tests is preserved. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The fastest is the ALLYLIC bromide — the six-membered ring carrying one \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bond, with the bromine on the carbon NEXT TO it. That compound is 3-bromocyclohexene.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set by how easily the CARBOCATION forms, so the question is which cation is the most stable. An allylic cation is delocalised over two carbons by resonance, which is a large stabilisation and one that no simple alkyl cation can match.

Ranking the rest: the plain cyclohexyl bromide is SECONDARY, the \(\mathrm{-CH_2Br}\) compound is PRIMARY, and the fully aromatic one is bromobenzene, an ARYL halide.

The aryl halide is not merely the slowest but effectively unreactive. The bromine's lone pair is delocalised into the ring, giving the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond partial double bond character, and the phenyl cation that would have to form is extremely unstable.

So the order runs allylic, secondary, primary, and aryl last by a wide margin.

rows.stem: Acetic acid reacts with \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) to give :
rows.solution:
Acetic acid with phosphorus pentachloride gives \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}COCl}\), ethanoyl chloride.

Phosphorus pentachloride replaces the HYDROXYL group of the carboxyl by chlorine; it does not touch the methyl group or the carbonyl oxygen:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{PCl_5} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COCl} + \mathrm{POCl_3} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The other options all involve substituting on the methyl carbon instead, which is a quite different reaction — chlorinating the \(\alpha\) position requires chlorine with red phosphorus, the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction, and would leave the carboxyl group intact.

Thionyl chloride does the same job as phosphorus pentachloride and is usually preferred, since its by-products are both gases and escape, leaving pure acid chloride.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: The formation of cyanohydrin from an aldehyde is an example of :
rows.solution:
Cyanohydrin formation is an example of NUCLEOPHILIC ADDITION.

The carbonyl carbon is electron deficient — oxygen is more electronegative and pulls the \(\pi\) electrons towards itself — so it attracts a NUCLEOPHILE. The cyanide ion attacks it, the \(\pi\) bond breaks with both electrons going to the oxygen, and the alkoxide formed then picks up a proton:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CN}\)

The process is an ADDITION, not a substitution, because nothing leaves the molecule: both fragments of hydrogen cyanide end up in the product, and the carbon changes from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\).

The contrast with an alkene is worth keeping. There the \(\pi\) bond is electron RICH and attracts electrophiles, so an alkene undergoes electrophilic addition while a carbonyl undergoes nucleophilic addition.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: In the Arrhenius equation, when log k is plotted against 1/T, a straight line is obtained whose :

options.label: B
options.text: slope is A and intercept is \(\dfrac{-\mathrm{E_a}}{\mathrm{R}}\).

options.label: C
options.text: slope is \(\dfrac{-\mathrm{E_a}}{\mathrm{RT}}\) and intercept is log A.

options.label: D
options.text: slope is \(\dfrac{-\,\mathrm{E_a}}{2{\cdot}303\,\mathrm{R}}\) and intercept is log A.

rows.solution:
The slope is \(\dfrac{-E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,R}\) and the intercept is \(\log A\).

Take logarithms of the Arrhenius equation \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\). With NATURAL logarithms,
\(\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}\)
and converting to COMMON logarithms by dividing through by 2.303,
\(\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T}\)

Compare with \(y = c + mx\), taking \(y\) as \(\log k\) and \(x\) as \(1/T\): the slope is \(-E_a/2{\cdot}303R\) and the intercept is \(\log A\).

The factor of 2.303 is exactly what distinguishes this from the natural-log version, where the slope would be \(-E_a/R\). And note that the slope cannot contain \(T\): temperature is the variable being plotted, so it cannot also sit inside a constant.

rows.stem: The reaction of an alkyl halide with sodium alkoxide forming ether is known as :
rows.solution:
The reaction is WILLIAMSON'S SYNTHESIS.

An alkyl halide is treated with a sodium alkoxide, and the alkoxide displaces the halide from the back in a single bimolecular step:
\(\mathrm{R{-}X} + \mathrm{R'{-}ONa} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'} + \mathrm{NaX}\)

Because the step is \(\mathrm{S_N}2\), the HALIDE must be primary; a tertiary halide has too crowded a carbon and the alkoxide — a strong base as well as a strong nucleophile — eliminates instead, giving an alkene. The method's value is that it makes UNSYMMETRICAL ethers, which cannot be had by simply dehydrating an alcohol.

Of the others, Wurtz couples two alkyl halides with sodium, Reimer-Tiemann puts an aldehyde group on phenol, and Kolbe's reaction puts a carboxyl group on it.

rows.stem: The correct order of the ease of dehydration of the following alcohols by the action of conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) is :
rows.solution:
The order is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C{-}OH} > \mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}OH} > \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}OH}\) — tertiary, then secondary, then primary.

Dehydration by concentrated sulphuric acid goes through a CARBOCATION. The acid protonates the hydroxyl group, water leaves, and the cation then loses a proton from the neighbouring carbon to give the alkene. The slow step is forming the cation, so the reactivity follows carbocation STABILITY.

A tertiary cation is stabilised by three alkyl groups releasing electron density towards it, a secondary by two, a primary by only one — hence the order.

The practical consequence is in the conditions each needs: a tertiary alcohol dehydrates in \(20\%\) sulphuric acid at about 358 K, while ethanol requires \(95\%\) acid at 443 K.

rows.stem: Which functional groups of glucose interact to form cyclic hemiacetal leading to pyranose structure ?

options.label: A
options.text: Aldehyde group and hydroxyl group at C – 4

options.label: B
options.text: Aldehyde group and hydroxyl group at C – 5

options.label: C
options.text: Ketone group and hydroxyl group at C – 4

options.label: D
options.text: Ketone group and hydroxyl group at C – 5

rows.solution:
The pyranose ring comes from the ALDEHYDE GROUP AND THE HYDROXYL GROUP AT \(\mathrm{C_5}\).

Glucose is an ALDOhexose, so its carbonyl is an aldehyde at \(\mathrm{C_1}\) — that alone rules out both options naming a ketone group. The hydroxyl on \(\mathrm{C_5}\) then adds across it to give a cyclic HEMIACETAL.

Count the ring members: \(\mathrm{C_1}\) through \(\mathrm{C_5}\) plus the bridging oxygen — a SIX membered ring, and it is its resemblance to pyran that gives the name.

Closing from \(\mathrm{C_4}\) instead would give a five membered furanose ring, which glucose can form but does not favour. Fructose is the contrast: being a KETOhexose with its carbonyl at \(\mathrm{C_2}\), it closes \(\mathrm{C_2}\) to \(\mathrm{C_5}\) and gets a furanose ring.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : When NaCl is added to water a depression in freezing point is observed.
Reason (R) : NaCl undergoes dissociation in water.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Adding sodium chloride to water does depress the freezing point, and sodium chloride does dissociate — both statements hold.

But dissociation is not WHY the depression occurs. Depression of freezing point is a COLLIGATIVE property: it happens with ANY non-volatile solute, dissociating or not. Adding glucose or urea, neither of which dissociates at all, lowers the freezing point just as surely. The cause is that solute particles lower the vapour pressure of the solvent, so a lower temperature is needed before solid and liquid have equal vapour pressures.

What dissociation changes is the MAGNITUDE. Each formula unit of sodium chloride gives two particles instead of one, so the depression is about twice what the same molality of glucose would give. The Reason explains how large the effect is, not why there is one.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Separation of Zr and Hf is difficult.
Reason (R) : Zr and Hf have similar radii due to lanthanoid contraction.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Zirconium and hafnium have almost identical atomic radii — about 160 pm each — although hafnium lies a whole period below zirconium and should therefore be considerably larger.

The cause is LANTHANOID CONTRACTION. The fourteen lanthanoids come between them in the periodic table, and across that series the \(4f\) electrons shield the growing nuclear charge very poorly, so the radius shrinks steadily. That shrinkage very nearly cancels the increase the extra period would otherwise bring.

Chemical separation depends on differences in size and in the properties that follow from it, so two elements of the same size in the same group behave almost identically and are notoriously hard to separate. The Reason therefore accounts for the Assertion completely.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) of ethanoic acid is lower than that of \(\mathrm{Cl-CH_2-COOH}\).
Reason (R) : Chlorine shows electron withdrawing (–I) effect which increases the acidic character of \(\mathrm{Cl-CH_2-COOH}\).
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

The Assertion has the comparison the wrong way round. A LOWER \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) means a STRONGER acid, and chloroethanoic acid is the stronger of the two — its \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) is about 2.86 against ethanoic acid's 4.76. So it is chloroethanoic acid whose \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) is lower, not ethanoic acid's.

The Reason is correct, and it is exactly why the Assertion fails. Chlorine is electronegative and withdraws electron density along the chain by its inductive effect. That pull helps disperse the negative charge on the carboxylate ion left behind after the proton leaves, so the anion is more stable and the proton departs more readily.

Corrected, the Reason would have explained the Assertion; as written it predicts the opposite.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aniline is a stronger base than ammonia.
Reason (R) : The unshared electron pair on nitrogen atom in aniline becomes less available for protonation due to resonance.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

Aniline is a WEAKER base than ammonia, not a stronger one — \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) about 9.4 against ammonia's 4.75, a difference of more than four orders of magnitude.

The Reason is correct, and it is precisely why. In aniline the nitrogen's lone pair is not confined to the nitrogen: it is delocalised INTO THE BENZENE RING by resonance, spread over the ortho and para carbons. A lone pair partly committed to the ring is less available to accept a proton, and the nitrogen is also attached to an \(sp^2\) carbon, which pulls density away from it as well.

Ammonia has no ring to absorb its lone pair, so that pair is fully available.

The Reason as written states the case AGAINST the Assertion, which is the signature of this answer.

rows.stem:
Calculate the potential of Iron electrode in which the concentration of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ion is \(0{\cdot}01\) M.
(\(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} = -\,0{\cdot}45\) V at 298 K)
[Given : log 10 = 1]
rows.solution:
A single electrode potential obeys the Nernst equation in the same form as a whole cell, with the metal ion in the denominator because the metal itself is a solid and does not appear:

\(E_{\mathrm{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]}\)

Two electrons are transferred, so \(n = 2\). With \([\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}] = 0{\cdot}01 = 10^{-2}\):
\(= -0{\cdot}45 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{10^{-2}}\)
\(= -0{\cdot}45 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times 2\log 10\)
\(= -0{\cdot}45 - 0{\cdot}059\)

\(E_{\mathrm{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} = -0{\cdot}509\ \mathrm{V}\)

The direction of the shift is the check on the work. Lowering the concentration of the metal ION makes the electrode a POORER oxidising agent — there is less of the species that would have to be reduced — so the potential must become more negative than the standard value, and it does.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Define molecularity of the reaction. State any one condition in which a bimolecular reaction may be kinetically of first order.
rows.solution:
MOLECULARITY is the number of reacting species — atoms, ions or molecules — that must COLLIDE SIMULTANEOUSLY in an elementary reaction for it to occur.

It is a THEORETICAL quantity, read off the proposed mechanism rather than measured, and it is defined only for an elementary reaction: a complex reaction is a sequence of steps, each possibly with its own molecularity, so the sequence as a whole has none. Being a count of colliding species, it must be a whole number and at least 1.

CONDITION FOR A BIMOLECULAR REACTION TO BE FIRST ORDER: when ONE OF THE REACTANTS IS PRESENT IN LARGE EXCESS.

Its concentration then barely changes as the reaction proceeds, so it can be treated as a constant and absorbed into the rate constant. What remains depends on one concentration alone. The acid hydrolysis of an ester is the standard instance, water being the solvent as well as a reactant:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\text{ester}][\mathrm{H_2O}] = k'[\text{ester}]\) with \(k' = k[\mathrm{H_2O}]\)

Such a reaction is called PSEUDO first order — bimolecular by its stoichiometry, first order by measurement.

rows.stem:
What happens when D-glucose is treated with the following reagents ?
(a) HI
(b) Conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) WITH HYDROGEN IODIDE and red phosphorus on prolonged heating, D-glucose is reduced all the way to N-HEXANE:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HI}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3}\)

Every oxygen is stripped out, and the product is a STRAIGHT chain of six carbons. That result is one of the classic proofs of glucose's structure: it shows that the six carbons are joined in an UNBRANCHED chain, since a branched skeleton would have given a branched hexane.

(b) WITH CONCENTRATED NITRIC ACID, a stronger oxidising agent than bromine water, BOTH ends of the molecule are oxidised — the aldehyde at \(\mathrm{C_1}\) and the primary alcohol at \(\mathrm{C_6}\) — giving the dicarboxylic acid SACCHARIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4COOH}\)

The contrast with bromine water is the point. That milder reagent touches only the aldehyde and gives gluconic acid, a MONOcarboxylic acid — which is how the presence of the primary hydroxyl at the far end is established separately.

rows.stem:
Draw the structures of major monohalo products in each of the following reactions :
(i) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH=CH_2} + \mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow\)
(ii) Cyclohexene \(+\ \mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\text{UV light}}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Both reactants are printed as DRAWN skeletal structures rather than named: (i) a Kekule benzene hexagon bearing a \(\mathrm{CH=CH_2}\) side chain, and (ii) a hexagon carrying one inner double-bond line on its right-hand edge. They are named in words above because naming a reactant cannot leak the answer, which is the product — but the real crop should be attached. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(i) Hydrogen bromide adds across the double bond of styrene, and the addition follows MARKOVNIKOV'S RULE — the proton goes to the carbon that already carries more hydrogens, so the bromine goes to the carbon attached to the RING.

The reason is the stability of the intermediate. Putting the positive charge on the benzylic carbon gives a cation delocalised into the ring by resonance; putting it on the terminal carbon would give a plain primary cation.

Product: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH(Br){-}CH_3}\), 1-bromo-1-phenylethane.

(ii) Bromine on cyclohexene under ULTRAVIOLET LIGHT is not an addition at all. Those conditions generate bromine RADICALS, and a radical abstracts a hydrogen rather than adding to the double bond. It takes the one most easily abstracted — the ALLYLIC hydrogen on the carbon next to the double bond — because the radical left behind is delocalised over the double bond.

Product: 3-bromocyclohexene, the ring keeping its double bond with \(\mathrm{Br}\) on the adjacent carbon.

In the dark, bromine would simply add across the double bond to give the 1,2-dibromide — but that is a dihalo product, and the question asks for monohalo.

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(i) Grignard reagent should be prepared under anhydrous conditions.
(ii) Alkyl halides give alcohol with aqueous KOH whereas in the presence of alcoholic KOH, alkenes are formed.
rows.solution:
(i) Because a GRIGNARD REAGENT REACTS WITH WATER, and the reagent is destroyed in doing so.

The carbon bonded to magnesium carries a large partial NEGATIVE charge — magnesium is far less electronegative than carbon — so that carbon behaves as a carbanion and is a powerful base. It seizes a proton from any acidic hydrogen it meets, and water's is acidic enough:
\(\mathrm{R{-}MgX} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}H} + \mathrm{Mg(OH)X}\)

The reagent ends up as an alkane, and none is left for the intended reaction. The same applies to alcohols, amines and carboxylic acids, so every trace of moisture must be excluded — the ether is dried and the apparatus kept under dry conditions.

(ii) Because the two reagents provide different attacking species, and each favours a different reaction.

AQUEOUS KOH supplies the hydroxide ion, which is a good NUCLEOPHILE in water. It attacks the carbon bearing the halogen and substitutes for it, giving the alcohol.

ALCOHOLIC KOH is different. The potassium hydroxide reacts with the alcohol to give ALKOXIDE ions, and an alkoxide is a much stronger BASE than hydroxide but a bulkier and poorer nucleophile. It therefore attacks a \(\beta\) HYDROGEN rather than the carbon, and the halide is eliminated along with it to give an alkene.

Substitution and elimination are always in competition; what the solvent changes is which one wins.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the chemical equation when :
(a) Butan-2-one is treated with Zn(Hg) and conc. HCl.
(b) Two molecules of benzaldehyde are treated with conc. NaOH.
rows.solution:
(a) Zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid is CLEMMENSEN REDUCTION, which converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\):
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. }\mathrm{HCl}]{\mathrm{Zn(Hg)}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
Butan-2-one becomes n-butane. Note the carbon skeleton is untouched — only the oxygen goes.

(b) Benzaldehyde has NO \(\alpha\)-hydrogen, so with concentrated alkali it cannot undergo aldol condensation and undergoes the CANNIZZARO reaction instead: two molecules react together, one being reduced to the alcohol and the other oxidised to the salt of the acid.
\(2\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \text{conc. }\mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH} + \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa}\)

It is a DISPROPORTIONATION — the same compound is both oxidised and reduced — which is possible only because there is no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen to open the easier aldol route.

rows.stem:
When a certain conductivity cell was filled with \(0{\cdot}05\) M KCl solution, it has a resistance of 100 ohm at \(25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). When the same cell was filled with \(0{\cdot}02\) M \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution, the resistance was 90 ohm. Calculate the conductivity and molar conductivity of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution.
(Given : Conductivity of \(0{\cdot}05\) M KCl solution \(= 1{\cdot}35 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{ohm^{-1}cm^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
The two measurements share one cell, so the potassium chloride solution is used to CALIBRATE it and the silver nitrate solution is then measured with the constant so obtained.

Step 1 — cell constant, from the solution of known conductivity:
\(G^{*} = \kappa \times R = 1{\cdot}35 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{ohm^{-1}cm^{-1}} \times 100\ \mathrm{ohm}\)
\(G^{*} = 1{\cdot}35\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

The units confirm the step: ohm cancels ohm\(^{-1}\), leaving reciprocal centimetres, which is what a cell constant must be.

Step 2 — conductivity of the silver nitrate solution, using the same constant with its own resistance:
\(\kappa = \dfrac{G^{*}}{R} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}35}{90}\)
\(\kappa = 0{\cdot}015\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\)

Step 3 — molar conductivity. Divide out the concentration to refer the conductivity to one mole of electrolyte:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}015 \times 1000}{0{\cdot}02}\)
\(\Lambda_m = 750\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The point of the two-stage method is that a cell's geometry cannot be measured accurately with a ruler, so it is determined once against a standard solution and then used for everything else.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The following initial rate data were obtained for the reaction :
\(2\mathrm{NO\,(g)} + \mathrm{Br_2\,(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NOBr\,(g)}\)

| Expt. No. | \(\mathrm{[NO]/mol\ L^{-1}}\) | \(\mathrm{[Br_2]/mol\ L^{-1}}\) | Initial Rate \(\mathrm{(mol\ L^{-1}\,s^{-1})}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(0{\cdot}05\) | \(0{\cdot}05\) | \(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}\) |
| 2 | \(0{\cdot}05\) | \(0{\cdot}15\) | \(3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}\) |
| 3 | \(0{\cdot}15\) | \(0{\cdot}05\) | \(9{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}\) |

(a) What is the order with respect to NO and \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) in the reaction ?
(b) Calculate the rate constant (k).
(c) Determine the rate of reaction when concentration of NO and \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) are \(0{\cdot}4\) M and \(0{\cdot}2\) M, respectively.
rows.solution:
(a) Compare the experiments in PAIRS, changing one concentration at a time.

Between experiments 1 and 2, \([\mathrm{Br_2}]\) trebles while \([\mathrm{NO}]\) is held fixed, and the rate trebles as well:
\(3 = 3^{q}\), so \(q = 1\) — FIRST order with respect to \(\mathrm{Br_2}\)

Between experiments 1 and 3, \([\mathrm{NO}]\) trebles while \([\mathrm{Br_2}]\) is held fixed, and the rate goes up NINE-fold:
\(9 = 3^{p}\), so \(p = 2\) — SECOND order with respect to \(\mathrm{NO}\)

The rate law is \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{Br_2}]\), overall order 3.

(b) Substitute experiment 1:
\(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3} = k\,(0{\cdot}05)^2(0{\cdot}05) = k \times 1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-4}\)
\(k = 8\ \mathrm{L^2\ mol^{-2}\ s^{-1}}\)

The unit is a check on the order: for third order the general form \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}L^{n-1}s^{-1}}\) gives exactly this.

(c) Apply the rate law to the new concentrations:
\(\text{Rate} = 8 \times (0{\cdot}4)^2 \times (0{\cdot}2) = 8 \times 0{\cdot}16 \times 0{\cdot}2\)
\(\text{Rate} = 2{\cdot}56 \times 10^{-1}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

Note that the order with respect to \(\mathrm{NO}\) happens to match its stoichiometric coefficient here, and the order with respect to \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) matches its own — but that agreement is something the DATA established, not something the equation could have told us.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the formula for the following coordination compound :
Potassium tetrahydroxidozincate (II)
(b) Arrange the following complexes in the increasing order of conductivity of their solution :
\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2}\), \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_3Cl_3]}\), \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\)
(c) Identify the type of isomerism exhibited by the following complexes :
(i) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5NO_2]^{2+}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]Cl_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Build the formula from the name. Tetrahydroxido means four \(\mathrm{OH^-}\), giving \(-4\); zinc is \(+2\), so the complex ion carries \(-2\) and needs two potassium ions outside:
\(\mathrm{K_2[Zn(OH)_4]}\)
The -ate ending on the metal is what tells you the complex is the ANION.

(b) Conductivity depends on HOW MANY IONS the compound gives in solution, so count them.

\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_3Cl_3]}\) — all three chlorides are inside the sphere, the complex is neutral, and NOTHING ionises: 0 ions.
\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2}\) — one chloride inside, two outside: 3 ions.
\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\) — all three outside: 4 ions.

Increasing order of conductivity:
\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_3Cl_3]} < \mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2} < \mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\)

These three are ionisation isomers of one another, and measuring conductivity is exactly how Werner distinguished such compounds.

(c)(i) LINKAGE ISOMERISM. The nitrite ion is AMBIDENTATE — it can bind through nitrogen, as nitro, or through oxygen, as nitrito — and the two forms are different compounds.

(ii) OPTICAL ISOMERISM. Three bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine ligands around an octahedral centre form a three-bladed propeller, which has no plane of symmetry and is therefore chiral, existing as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images.

rows.stem:
(a) Which of the following is an allylic halide ?
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-Br}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH(Br)-CH_3}\)
(b) Out of chlorobenzene and 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene, which is more reactive towards nucleophilic substitution and why ?
(c) Which isomer of \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Cl}\) has the lowest boiling point ?
rows.solution:
(a) The ALLYLIC halide is \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}CH(Br){-}CH_3}\).

An allylic halide has its halogen on an \(sp^3\) carbon that is ADJACENT to a double bond. Here the bromine sits on the third carbon while the double bond lies between the first and second — so the halogen-bearing carbon is next to the double bond, not part of it.

The other compound, \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH{=}CH{-}Br}\), is VINYLIC: its bromine is attached directly TO a doubly bonded carbon. The distinction matters greatly in practice — an allylic halide is exceptionally reactive, its cation being resonance stabilised, while a vinylic halide is among the least reactive of all, its \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond having partial double bond character.

(b) 2,4,6-TRINITROCHLOROBENZENE is far more reactive.

The three NITRO groups are strongly ELECTRON WITHDRAWING, and their positions are what make them effective. Nucleophilic substitution here goes through a negatively charged carbanion intermediate, and a nitro group at the ORTHO or PARA position can accept that negative charge onto its own oxygen by resonance. Three such groups stabilise the intermediate enormously, so the energy barrier falls.

Chlorobenzene has no such help. It is hydrolysed only at about 623 K under 300 atmospheres; 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene is hydrolysed by warm water alone.

(c) TERT-BUTYL CHLORIDE, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C{-}Cl}\), has the lowest boiling point.

All four isomers of \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Cl}\) have the same molecular mass, so the difference lies in SHAPE. Boiling point depends on van der Waals forces, and those depend on how much surface two molecules can present to each other. The more BRANCHED an isomer, the more nearly spherical it is, the smaller its surface area, and the weaker the forces between its molecules.

Tert-butyl chloride is the most branched of the four, so it boils lowest; n-butyl chloride, the straight chain, boils highest.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the mechanism of the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[443\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{CH_2=CH_2}\)
(b) Write the main product in each of the following reactions :
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH=CH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{b)\ 3H_2O_2/OH^-}]{\mathrm{a)\ B_2H_6}}\)
(ii) Phenol \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{b)\ CO_2,\ H^+}]{\mathrm{a)\ aq.\ NaOH}}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — In sub-part (b)(ii) the starting material is printed as a DRAWN structure — a Kekule benzene hexagon bearing \(\mathrm{OH}\) — not named. It is named 'Phenol' above because the answer asked for is the PRODUCT, so naming the substrate leaks nothing; the real crop should still be attached. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
(a) MECHANISM OF DEHYDRATION OF ETHANOL, in three steps.

Step 1 — formation of the protonated alcohol. The oxygen uses a lone pair to pick up a proton from the acid. This step is FAST and reversible:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}OH} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)
The product is the ethyl oxonium ion. Its purpose is to convert a poor leaving group into a good one — water.

Step 2 — formation of the carbocation. The protonated alcohol loses water. This is the SLOW step and therefore the rate determining one, because a bond breaks and a charged species is created:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 3 — elimination of a proton. A base removes a proton from the carbon next to the positive centre, and the pair of electrons left behind forms the double bond, regenerating the catalyst:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H^+}\)

The temperature selects the product: at 413 K a second alcohol molecule attacks the protonated one instead, and the product is ethoxyethane rather than ethene.

(b)(i) Diborane followed by alkaline hydrogen peroxide is HYDROBORATION-OXIDATION, and it adds water across the double bond ANTI-Markovnikov — the hydroxyl goes to the carbon with MORE hydrogens, because boron, being the bulkier and less electronegative atom, attaches to the less hindered carbon.
Product: \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH}\), butan-1-ol.
Acid-catalysed hydration of the same alkene would have given butan-2-ol instead, which is what makes this route worth having.

(ii) Phenol with aqueous sodium hydroxide followed by carbon dioxide and acid is KOLBE'S REACTION. The alkali converts phenol to the more strongly activated phenoxide ion, which attacks carbon dioxide at its ORTHO position; acidification then frees the acid.
Product: SALICYLIC ACID, 2-hydroxybenzoic acid — a benzene ring carrying \(-\mathrm{OH}\) and \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) on adjacent carbons.

rows.stem:
Answer the following : (any three)
(a) What is peptide linkage ?
(b) What type of bonds hold a DNA double helix together ?
(c) Which one of the following is a polysaccharide ?
Sucrose, Glucose, Starch, Fructose
(d) Give one example each for water-soluble vitamins and fat-soluble vitamins.
rows.solution:
(a) A PEPTIDE LINKAGE is the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CO-NH}-\) that joins two amino acids. The carboxyl group of one condenses with the amino group of the next, a molecule of water is lost, and the bond formed between that carbon and that nitrogen is the peptide linkage. It is what builds a protein from its residues.

(b) HYDROGEN BONDS hold the two strands of a DNA double helix together. They form between specific pairs of bases — adenine with thymine through two such bonds, guanine with cytosine through three — which is what makes the two strands complementary rather than identical.

(c) STARCH is the polysaccharide. Glucose and fructose are MONOsaccharides, single sugar units; sucrose is a DISaccharide, one glucose joined to one fructose. Starch is a polymer of hundreds of glucose units, in two forms — linear amylose and branched amylopectin.

(d) WATER SOLUBLE: vitamin C, or any of the B group. FAT SOLUBLE: vitamin A, or D, E or K.

The distinction is not a chemical curiosity. Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the liver and adipose tissue, so a reserve accumulates; water-soluble ones are excreted in the urine and must be supplied regularly in the diet.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Compound (A) \(\mathrm{(C_6H_{12}O_2)}\) on reduction with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) gives two compounds (B) and (C). The compound (B) on oxidation with PCC gives compound (D) which upon treatment with dilute NaOH and subsequent heating gives compound (E). Compound (E) on catalytic hydrogenation gives compound (C). The compound (D) is oxidized further to give compound (F) which is found to be a monobasic acid (Molecular weight = 60). Identify the compounds (A), (B), (C), (D), (E) and (F).
rows.solution:
Work from the END of the chain, where the clue is quantitative.

Compound \(\mathrm{F}\) is a MONOBASIC acid of molecular weight 60. Only one acid fits: \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), ethanoic acid, at \(24 + 4 + 32 = 60\).
\(\mathrm{F} = \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

\(\mathrm{D}\) is oxidised to that acid, so \(\mathrm{D}\) is the corresponding aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{D} = \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), ethanal

\(\mathrm{B}\) gives \(\mathrm{D}\) with PCC, and PCC stops a primary alcohol at the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\), ethanol

\(\mathrm{D}\) with dilute alkali and then heat is the ALDOL CONDENSATION — two molecules of ethanal join and the product then loses water:
\(\mathrm{E} = \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCHO}\), but-2-enal

Catalytic hydrogenation of \(\mathrm{E}\) reduces both the double bond and the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH}\), butan-1-ol

\(\mathrm{A}\) is \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_2}\) and gives TWO alcohols with lithium aluminium hydride, which is the signature of an ESTER — reduction gives the alcohol from the acid part and the alcohol from the alkoxy part. The two alcohols are ethanol and butan-1-ol, and \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_2}\) has mass 116:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3COOCH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3}\), butyl ethanoate

The mirror-image ester \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2COOCH_2CH_3}\), ethyl butanoate, also has the formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_2}\) and also reduces to the same two alcohols — the data given cannot distinguish them, so either is acceptable.

rows.stem: How do primary batteries differ from secondary batteries ?
rows.context:
Batteries and fuel cells are very useful forms of galvanic cell. Any battery or cell that we use as a source of electrical energy is basically a galvanic cell. However, for a battery to be of practical use it should be reasonably light, compact and its voltage should not vary appreciably during its use. There are mainly two types of batteries — primary batteries and secondary batteries.
In the primary batteries, the reaction occurs only once and after use over a period of time the battery becomes dead and cannot be reused again, whereas the secondary batteries are rechargeable.
Production of electricity by thermal plants is not a very efficient method and is a major source of pollution. To solve this problem, galvanic cells are designed in such a way that energy of combustion of fuels is directly converted into electrical energy, and these are known as fuel cells. One such fuel cell was used in the Apollo space programme.
rows.solution:
A PRIMARY battery cannot be recharged; a SECONDARY battery can.

In a primary cell the reaction is effectively irreversible. Once the reactants sealed inside are used up the cell is dead and is discarded — the dry cell and the mercury cell are examples.

In a secondary cell the reaction CAN be driven backwards. Applying an external voltage greater than the cell's own forces current through in the opposite direction, the electrode reactions reverse, and the original reactants are restored. The lead storage battery and the nickel-cadmium cell are the standard examples, and both can be charged and discharged a great many times.

rows.stem: The cell potential of Mercury cell is \(1{\cdot}35\) V, and remains constant during its life. Give reason.
rows.context:
Batteries and fuel cells are very useful forms of galvanic cell. Any battery or cell that we use as a source of electrical energy is basically a galvanic cell. However, for a battery to be of practical use it should be reasonably light, compact and its voltage should not vary appreciably during its use. There are mainly two types of batteries — primary batteries and secondary batteries.
In the primary batteries, the reaction occurs only once and after use over a period of time the battery becomes dead and cannot be reused again, whereas the secondary batteries are rechargeable.
Production of electricity by thermal plants is not a very efficient method and is a major source of pollution. To solve this problem, galvanic cells are designed in such a way that energy of combustion of fuels is directly converted into electrical energy, and these are known as fuel cells. One such fuel cell was used in the Apollo space programme.
rows.solution:
Because the overall reaction of the mercury cell involves NO ION IN SOLUTION whose concentration changes.

The potential of any cell obeys the Nernst equation, and it drifts as the cell runs only when the reaction quotient shifts — that is, when the reaction consumes or produces something whose concentration appears in that quotient.

The mercury cell's reaction is
\(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)} + \mathrm{HgO(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ZnO(s)} + \mathrm{Hg(l)}\)
and every species in it is a SOLID or a pure liquid, none of which enters the quotient at all. With nothing to shift, the potential stays at \(1{\cdot}35\) V for the life of the cell.

The dry cell is the contrast: its reaction produces and consumes ions in the paste, so its voltage falls steadily as it is used. The mercury cell's steady voltage is what suits it to hearing aids and watches.

rows.stem: Write the reactions involved in the recharging of the lead storage battery.
rows.context:
Batteries and fuel cells are very useful forms of galvanic cell. Any battery or cell that we use as a source of electrical energy is basically a galvanic cell. However, for a battery to be of practical use it should be reasonably light, compact and its voltage should not vary appreciably during its use. There are mainly two types of batteries — primary batteries and secondary batteries.
In the primary batteries, the reaction occurs only once and after use over a period of time the battery becomes dead and cannot be reused again, whereas the secondary batteries are rechargeable.
Production of electricity by thermal plants is not a very efficient method and is a major source of pollution. To solve this problem, galvanic cells are designed in such a way that energy of combustion of fuels is directly converted into electrical energy, and these are known as fuel cells. One such fuel cell was used in the Apollo space programme.
rows.solution:
Recharging drives the discharge reactions BACKWARDS, so both electrodes shed the lead sulphate that coated them during use. An external voltage greater than the battery's own is applied, and the cell now works as an ELECTROLYTIC cell.

At the electrode where REDUCTION now occurs — the cathode of the electrolytic cell — lead sulphate is reduced back to lead:
\(\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)}\)

At the electrode where OXIDATION now occurs, lead sulphate is oxidised back to lead dioxide:
\(\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)} + 4\mathrm{H^+(aq)} + 2e^-\)

Sulphuric acid is regenerated in the process, which is why the density of the electrolyte rises again as charging proceeds — and why that density is used as a gauge of how charged a battery is.

rows.stem: Write two advantages of fuel cells over other galvanic cells.
rows.context:
Batteries and fuel cells are very useful forms of galvanic cell. Any battery or cell that we use as a source of electrical energy is basically a galvanic cell. However, for a battery to be of practical use it should be reasonably light, compact and its voltage should not vary appreciably during its use. There are mainly two types of batteries — primary batteries and secondary batteries.
In the primary batteries, the reaction occurs only once and after use over a period of time the battery becomes dead and cannot be reused again, whereas the secondary batteries are rechargeable.
Production of electricity by thermal plants is not a very efficient method and is a major source of pollution. To solve this problem, galvanic cells are designed in such a way that energy of combustion of fuels is directly converted into electrical energy, and these are known as fuel cells. One such fuel cell was used in the Apollo space programme.
rows.solution:
TWO ADVANTAGES of fuel cells:

HIGH EFFICIENCY, around 70%. The chemical energy of the fuel is converted DIRECTLY into electrical energy instead of passing through heat and a mechanical stage, so the cell is not limited by the Carnot efficiency that caps any heat engine. A thermal power station managing about 40% is the comparison.

POLLUTION FREE. The hydrogen-oxygen cell produces only WATER — no oxides of carbon, nitrogen or sulphur, and no particulates. On the Apollo flights the water produced was drunk by the crew.

A third advantage, if one is wanted: the cell does not run down, because its reactants are supplied continuously from outside rather than stored within it, so it works as long as it is fed.

rows.stem: What is crystal field splitting energy ?
rows.context: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds whereas 'The Crystal Field Theory' for coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. The crystal field theory attributes the colour of the coordination compounds to d-d transition of the electron. Coordination compounds find extensive applications in metallurgical processes, analytical and medicinal chemistry.
rows.solution:
CRYSTAL FIELD SPLITTING ENERGY is the ENERGY DIFFERENCE between the two sets of d orbitals that the ligands create.

In a free metal ion the five d orbitals are degenerate — all of the same energy. Bring ligands up to it and their negative charge repels the d electrons, but unequally: the orbitals pointing straight at the ligands are raised more than those pointing between them. In an octahedral field the set splits into a lower \(t_{2g}\) group of three and an upper \(e_g\) group of two, and the gap between them is written \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\).

Its size depends on the ligand — which is what the spectrochemical series orders — and on the metal's oxidation state. It is \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) that a d-d transition must cross, so it sets the colour; and comparing it with the pairing energy decides whether the complex is high or low spin.

rows.stem: Give reason for the violet colour of the complex \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) on the basis of crystal field theory.
rows.context: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds whereas 'The Crystal Field Theory' for coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. The crystal field theory attributes the colour of the coordination compounds to d-d transition of the electron. Coordination compounds find extensive applications in metallurgical processes, analytical and medicinal chemistry.
rows.solution:
Titanium in this complex is \(+3\), so \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is \(3d^1\) — a single d electron.

The six water ligands split the five d orbitals into a lower \(t_{2g}\) set and an upper \(e_g\) set. That single electron occupies \(t_{2g}\), and it can absorb a photon of visible light and jump to \(e_g\):
\(t_{2g}^1\,e_g^0 \longrightarrow t_{2g}^0\,e_g^1\)

That is a d-d TRANSITION, and the energy it requires corresponds to the YELLOW-GREEN part of the spectrum. Those wavelengths are absorbed, so what passes through to the eye is the complementary colour — VIOLET.

Heating the complex drives off the water ligands, and with no ligands there is no crystal field, no splitting, no transition and no colour: the compound becomes colourless.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is paramagnetic while \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) is diamagnetic. Explain why. [Atomic No. : Cr = 24, Ni = 28]
rows.context: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds whereas 'The Crystal Field Theory' for coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. The crystal field theory attributes the colour of the coordination compounds to d-d transition of the electron. Coordination compounds find extensive applications in metallurgical processes, analytical and medicinal chemistry.
rows.solution:
Both answers come from counting unpaired electrons, and the ligands decide the count.

\(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\). Chromium is atomic number 24, so the neutral atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1\); the six ammonia molecules are neutral, so chromium is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) is \(3d^3\).

Three electrons in a set of five orbitals occupy three of them SINGLY, whatever the ligand — there is no pairing decision to make, because there are more orbitals than electrons. The \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement leaves THREE unpaired electrons, so the complex is PARAMAGNETIC, with \(\mu = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = 3{\cdot}87\) B.M.

\(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\). Nickel is atomic number 28; four cyanides give \(-4\) against an overall \(-2\), so nickel is \(+2\) and \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\), which would normally leave two unpaired electrons.

But cyanide is a STRONG FIELD ligand. It forces those two to pair, leaving all eight electrons paired and ONE \(3d\) orbital free; that orbital with the \(4s\) and two \(4p\) gives \(dsp^2\) hybridisation and a square planar shape. With no unpaired electron the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

rows.stem:
Explain why \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) is an inner orbital complex, whereas \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) is an outer orbital complex.
[Atomic No. : Fe = 26]
rows.context: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds whereas 'The Crystal Field Theory' for coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields. The crystal field theory attributes the colour of the coordination compounds to d-d transition of the electron. Coordination compounds find extensive applications in metallurgical processes, analytical and medicinal chemistry.
rows.solution:
Iron is atomic number 26, so the neutral atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^6 4s^2\). In both complexes iron is \(+3\) — six cyanides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), and six waters are neutral against an overall \(+3\) — so in each case the ion is \(3d^5\).

The configuration is the same; the LIGAND is what differs.

\(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\). Cyanide is a STRONG FIELD ligand: the splitting it produces exceeds the pairing energy, so the five electrons crowd into the three lower \(t_{2g}\) orbitals rather than spreading out. That leaves TWO INNER \(3d\) orbitals empty, and bonding uses them together with the \(4s\) and \(4p\) — hybridisation \(d^2sp^3\). Because the d orbitals used belong to the INNER \(3d\) shell, this is an INNER ORBITAL complex, and it is low spin, with one unpaired electron.

\(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\). Water is a WEAK FIELD ligand: its splitting is smaller than the pairing energy, so all five electrons stay unpaired, one in each \(3d\) orbital. No inner \(3d\) orbital is left vacant, and bonding must reach OUTWARDS to the \(4d\) set — hybridisation \(sp^3d^2\). That makes it an OUTER ORBITAL complex, high spin, with five unpaired electrons.

The names simply record which d orbitals the hybridisation used.

rows.stem:
(i) At the same temperature, \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) gas is more soluble in water than \(\mathrm{O_2}\) gas. Which one of them will have higher value of \(\mathrm{K_H}\) and why ?
(ii) How does the size of blood cells change when placed in an aqueous solution containing more than \(0{\cdot}9\%\) (mass/volume) sodium chloride ?
(iii) 1 molal aqueous solution of an electrolyte \(\mathrm{A_2B_3}\) is 60% ionized. Calculate the boiling point of the solution.
(Given : \(\mathrm{K_b}\) for \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) \(= 0{\cdot}52\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
(i) OXYGEN has the higher Henry's law constant.

Rearranging \(p = K_{\mathrm{H}}x\) gives \(x = p/K_{\mathrm{H}}\), so at a given pressure the mole fraction dissolved is INVERSELY proportional to \(K_{\mathrm{H}}\): a larger constant means a LESS soluble gas.

Carbon dioxide is the more soluble of the two — it reacts with water to some extent as well as dissolving physically — so it must have the SMALLER constant, and oxygen the larger.

(ii) The blood cells SHRINK.

Blood is isotonic with \(0{\cdot}9\%\) sodium chloride, so a solution stronger than that is HYPERTONIC. Water then flows OUT of the cells, through their membranes, towards the more concentrated solution outside. The cells lose water and shrivel, a process called crenation.

A solution weaker than \(0{\cdot}9\%\) does the opposite: water flows in and the cells swell and may burst. This is why intravenous fluids must be isotonic with blood.

(iii) \(\mathrm{A_2B_3}\) ionises into 2 cations and 3 anions, so \(n = 5\).

From the degree of ionisation:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{n - 1}\), so \(0{\cdot}6 = \dfrac{i - 1}{5 - 1}\)
\(i - 1 = 2{\cdot}4\), giving \(i = 3{\cdot}4\)

Then the elevation of boiling point:
\(\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m = 3{\cdot}4 \times 0{\cdot}52 \times 1 = 1{\cdot}768\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(T_b = 373 + 1{\cdot}768 = 374{\cdot}768\ \mathrm{K}\)

Taking the boiling point of water as \(373{\cdot}15\) K instead gives \(374{\cdot}918\) K; the elevation itself is \(1{\cdot}768\) K either way.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
(i) The vapour pressures of A and B at \(25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) are 75 mm Hg and 25 mm Hg, respectively. If A and B are mixed such that the mole fraction of A in the mixture is \(0{\cdot}4\), then calculate the mole fraction of B in vapour phase.
(ii) Define colligative property. Which colligative property is preferred for the molar mass determination of macromolecules ?
(iii) Why are equimolar solutions of sodium chloride and glucose not isotonic ?
rows.solution:
(i) Find the total pressure first, then the composition of the vapour above it.

The mole fraction of \(\mathrm{A}\) is 0.4, so that of \(\mathrm{B}\) is 0.6. By Raoult's law:
\(p_{\mathrm{A}} = 75 \times 0{\cdot}4 = 30\) mm Hg
\(p_{\mathrm{B}} = 25 \times 0{\cdot}6 = 15\) mm Hg
\(p_{\text{total}} = 30 + 15 = 45\) mm Hg

By Dalton's law, a component's mole fraction IN THE VAPOUR is its partial pressure divided by the total:
\(y_{\mathrm{B}} = \dfrac{p_{\mathrm{B}}}{p_{\text{total}}} = \dfrac{15}{45} = \dfrac{1}{3}\)

\(y_{\mathrm{B}} = 0{\cdot}33\)

A mole fraction is a ratio of two pressures, so it is a pure NUMBER and carries no unit [the marking scheme prints "mm Hg" after this value; that is a slip, and the two pressures have already cancelled].

Note that \(\mathrm{B}\) makes up 0.6 of the liquid but only 0.33 of the vapour — the vapour is richer in the MORE VOLATILE component, which is \(\mathrm{A}\). That enrichment is the whole basis of fractional distillation.

(ii) A COLLIGATIVE PROPERTY is one that depends on the NUMBER of solute particles in solution and not on their nature. The four are relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point, and osmotic pressure.

For MACROMOLECULES the property preferred is OSMOTIC PRESSURE. A protein or polymer has an enormous molar mass, so even a substantial mass of it gives very few moles and every colligative effect is tiny; the freezing point depression would be a few thousandths of a degree. Osmotic pressure is large and readily measured even for a very dilute solution, and it is measured at room temperature, so the sample is not heated and does not denature.

(iii) Because SODIUM CHLORIDE DISSOCIATES IN WATER AND GLUCOSE DOES NOT.

Osmotic pressure is \(\Pi = iCRT\), and it counts PARTICLES, not formula units. Each formula unit of sodium chloride gives two ions, so \(i = 2\); glucose dissolves as whole molecules, so \(i = 1\).

Equimolar solutions therefore hold twice as many particles in the salt solution as in the sugar one, and its osmotic pressure is about twice as great. Two solutions are isotonic only when their osmotic pressures are EQUAL, which these are not.

rows.stem:
Answer any five questions of the following :
(a) N,N-diethyl-benzenesulphonamide is insoluble in alkali. Give reason.
(b) Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction. Why ?
(c) Write a simple chemical test to distinguish between methylamine and aniline.
(d) Write the chemical reaction involved in Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.
(e) How will you convert aniline to p-bromoaniline ?
(f) Complete the following reaction :
Benzenediazonium chloride \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)\ NaNO_2\,/\,Cu,\ \Delta}]{\mathrm{(i)\ HBF_4}}\)
(g) Write the structures of A and B in the following reaction :
Benzoic acid \(\xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2 + NaOH}} \mathrm{B}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Two sub-parts print DRAWN structures as their starting material rather than naming it: (f) a Kekule benzene hexagon bearing \(\mathrm{N_2^+Cl^-}\), and (g) a Kekule benzene hexagon bearing \(\mathrm{COOH}\). Both are named in words above because the answers asked for are the products, so naming the substrates leaks nothing; the real crops should still be attached. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
(a) Because N,N-diethylbenzenesulphonamide has NO HYDROGEN LEFT ON ITS NITROGEN.

In a sulphonamide made from a PRIMARY amine, one hydrogen remains on the nitrogen, and the two electron-withdrawing oxygens of the sulphonyl group beside it make that hydrogen acidic — so alkali removes it and the compound dissolves as its sodium salt.

Here the amine was TERTIARY in effect: both positions on the nitrogen are taken by ethyl groups. With no acidic hydrogen there is nothing for the alkali to remove, so the compound is not acidic and stays insoluble.

(b) Because ANILINE FORMS A SALT WITH ALUMINIUM CHLORIDE, the Lewis acid used as catalyst.

The nitrogen's lone pair is exactly what a Lewis acid seeks, so the catalyst bonds to it and is tied up. Worse, the nitrogen is now positively charged, and a positively charged group is strongly DEACTIVATING and meta directing — so the ring is far less able to attack an electrophile than aniline itself would be.

(c) Use the AZO DYE TEST. Treat each with nitrous acid at 273-278 K, then add the product to an alkaline solution of phenol.

ANILINE, an aromatic primary amine, forms a diazonium salt stable at that temperature, and coupling it with phenol gives a brilliant ORANGE dye. METHYLAMINE, an aliphatic primary amine, forms a diazonium salt that decomposes at once with brisk effervescence of NITROGEN, leaving nothing to couple — so no dye appears.

The nitrogen gas itself is the simpler observation: methylamine gives it, aniline does not until warmed.

(d) GABRIEL PHTHALIMIDE SYNTHESIS, in three steps:
\(\text{phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KOH}} \text{potassium phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{R{-}X}} \text{N-alkylphthalimide} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \text{sodium phthalate}\)

Potassium hydroxide removes the imide's acidic \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogen, the anion displaces halide from the alkyl halide, and hydrolysis then frees the amine. The method's whole value is that it gives a PURE PRIMARY amine with no secondary or tertiary contamination — unlike ammonolysis of an alkyl halide, which gives a mixture. It fails for aromatic amines, because an aryl halide will not undergo that substitution.

(e) ANILINE TO p-BROMOANILINE, in three steps, and the first is PROTECTION.

Bromine water alone would give 2,4,6-tribromoaniline, because the amino group is so strongly activating. Acetylating it first moderates that activation, so only one bromine goes on and it goes para:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{pyridine}]{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]{\mathrm{Br_2}} \mathrm{p\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}\ \text{or}\ \mathrm{OH^-}} \mathrm{p\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NH_2}\)

(f) The product is NITROBENZENE.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)}\ \mathrm{NaNO_2}/\mathrm{Cu},\ \Delta]{\mathrm{(i)}\ \mathrm{HBF_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} + \mathrm{N_2}\)
Fluoroboric acid first precipitates the diazonium fluoroborate; warming that with sodium nitrite and copper powder replaces the diazonium group by a nitro group. Heating the fluoroborate ALONE would give fluorobenzene instead — the Balz-Schiemann reaction — so the second reagent is what decides the product.

(g) Heating benzoic acid with ammonia gives the ammonium salt and then the AMIDE; Hofmann bromamide degradation then converts that amide to a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2}\), benzamide
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Account for the following :
(1) The melting and boiling points of Zn, Cd and Hg are low.
(2) Of the \(\mathrm{d^4}\) species, \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is strongly reducing while \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is strongly oxidizing.
(3) \(\mathrm{E^{o}}\) value of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}\) is \(+\,0{\cdot}34\) V.
(ii) Complete and balance the following chemical equations :
(1) \(\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}}\)
(2) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 6\,\mathrm{I^-} + 14\,\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(i)(1) Because zinc, cadmium and mercury have COMPLETELY FILLED d orbitals, so those electrons take no part in the metallic bonding.

Each is \(d^{10}s^2\) as the atom, with NO unpaired d electrons. Only the two \(s\) electrons are available for bonding, so the interatomic forces are weak, and melting or boiling these metals takes correspondingly little energy — mercury is a liquid at room temperature, and zinc melts at 693 K against chromium's 2130 K.

This is the same reason they are not counted as transition elements at all.

(2) Both are \(d^4\) species, and in each case the driving force is the STABILITY OF THE NEIGHBOURING ION.

\(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is strongly REDUCING because losing one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\) — in an octahedral field the stable half-filled \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement. Chromium(II) therefore gives that electron up readily, which is what being a reducing agent means.

\(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is strongly OXIDISING because GAINING one electron gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — an exactly half-filled subshell, and unusually stable. Manganese(III) therefore takes an electron readily.

The two ions have the same d count and behave oppositely, because what each is reaching for lies on a different side.

(3) Because the energy REQUIRED to take copper from the metal to the aqueous ion is not repaid by the energy released in hydrating it.

\(E^{\circ}\) for \(\mathrm{M^{2+}/M}\) reflects the balance of three steps: atomising the metal, ionising the atom, and hydrating the ion. Copper has an unusually HIGH enthalpy of atomisation and a LOW enthalpy of hydration for its \(+2\) ion, so the sum comes out unfavourable. The metal resists going into solution as its ion, and the potential is POSITIVE — \(+0{\cdot}34\) V, the only positive value in the first transition series.

The practical consequence is that copper does NOT liberate hydrogen from acids; it dissolves only in acids that are also oxidising, such as nitric acid.

(ii)(1) Heating potassium permanganate decomposes it, manganese ending in two different oxidation states, \(+6\) and \(+4\):
\(2\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

(2) Dichromate oxidises iodide to iodine in acid, chromium falling from \(+6\) to \(+3\):
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 6\mathrm{I^-} + 14\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{I_2} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Six electrons change hands: two chromiums take three each, and six iodides give up one each.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Out of \(\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CuCl_2}\), which is more stable in aqueous solution and why ?
(ii) Write the general electronic configuration of f-block elements.
(iii) Predict which of the following will be coloured in aqueous solution and why ?
\(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\)
[Atomic number : Sc = 21, Fe = 26, Zn = 30]
(iv) How can you obtain potassium dichromate from sodium chromate ?
(v) Why do transition metals and their compounds show catalytic activities ?
rows.solution:
(i) \(\mathrm{CuCl_2}\) is the more stable in aqueous solution.

Copper(I) is unstable in water and DISPROPORTIONATES — the same ion is oxidised and reduced at once:
\(2\mathrm{Cu^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

The reason is hydration energy. \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) carries twice the charge on a smaller ion, so it is hydrated far more strongly than \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\), and that extra energy more than pays for the second ionisation. In the SOLID state, where there is no water to do the hydrating, copper(I) compounds are perfectly stable.

(ii) General electronic configuration of the f-block:
\((n-2)f^{1-14}\ (n-1)d^{0-1}\ ns^2\)

The \(f\) orbitals of the antepenultimate shell are being filled, which is why these are called INNER transition elements. The \(d\) exponent is 0 or 1 because an electron occasionally goes into the \(d\) orbital instead, when doing so reaches an empty, half-filled or filled \(f\) subshell.

(iii) \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) alone is COLOURED.

Colour requires a PARTLY FILLED d subshell, so that an electron can absorb visible light and jump between the split sets. Work out each: \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(3d^0\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\), and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\).

Only iron(III) has unpaired d electrons with vacancies to move into. Scandium(III) has no d electron at all and zinc(II) has a completely filled set with no vacancy — so both are colourless, which is why scandium and zinc compounds are white.

(iv) Two steps. First acidify the sodium chromate, which shifts the chromate-dichromate equilibrium:
\(2\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Then treat the sodium dichromate with potassium chloride:
\(\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)

The second step works because potassium dichromate is much LESS soluble than the sodium salt, so it crystallises out as it forms and the equilibrium is pulled across.

(v) Because of their VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES and their ability to form COMPLEXES.

A catalyst works by offering a lower-energy path, and a transition metal does that by accepting electrons from one reactant and passing them to another — moving between oxidation states and returning to its original state at the end. Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process works exactly this way.

The second mechanism is surface adsorption. A transition metal has vacant d orbitals that can bind reactant molecules to its surface, holding them close together and weakening their bonds. Finely divided metals also provide a large surface area, which is why iron is used as a powder in the Haber process.
